s1.quote: rests on her starboard side at a depth of 160 feet (49 m)
She sits upright on the seafloor in 100 feet (30 meters) of water.
At 115 feet (35 m) below the surface, U-701 is still intact, retaining its 8.8 cm (3.5 in) deck gun.

s2.quote: the largely intact U-701 lies 115 feet deep, mired in the ever-undulating shoals off Cape Hatteras.

s3.quote: visibility also varies, but commonly ranges from 10 to 40 feet (3 to 12 m). … the strength of the ocean currents on the site vary widely from slight to very swift.

highlights.text: Largely intact U-boat with 88 mm deck gun

hazards.text: Shifting sand can bury the wreck; currents vary widely

summary.text: A World War II German submarine sunk by aircraft in 1942 and lying largely intact in the shoals off Cape Hatteras. Sand and current decide whether it is visible on a given day, but the deck gun can still be seen when conditions allow.

sites.name: SS City of Rio de Janeiro

s1.quote: The wreck lies in 287 feet (87 m) of water just off the Golden Gate … the currents are too strong and the water too deep for anyone other than professional divers.

s2.publisher: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries
s2.quote: lies 287 feet below the surface just outside the Golden Gate, not far from where it ran aground in 1901.

hazards.text: Strong currents and great depth off the Golden Gate

summary.text: The 1901 passenger steamer lies deep off the Golden Gate, found again by NOAA sonar surveys. Depth and strong currents put it beyond ordinary recreational diving; it is a site for technical or professional teams.

sites.name: USS Arthur W. Radford
sites.depthNote: Reef site depth 120-140 ft; Radford listed near 130 ft

s1.quote: lies upright down in about 100 feet (30 m) of water. … a popular night dive

highlights.text: Popular night dive and lobster wreck

s1.quote: The shipwreck lies in 28 feet (8.5 m) of water about one mile (1.6 km) offshore of Fort Macon State Park
more than 91 feet (28 m) of water, landing upright on the river bottom … Between April and December, a large blue and white mooring buoy is anchored about 70 feet (21 m) from the wreck

s2.quote: It lies upright in more than 90 feet of water with about 65 feet over its conning tower. … Advanced dive only: deep water, near-zero visibility, strong currents.

access.value: Maryland historic shipwreck preserve; no commercial charters operate there

summary.text: A German Type VII submarine sunk in the Potomac after the war and now Maryland's first historic shipwreck preserve. It sits upright in deep, dark, current-swept water, so it is an advanced dive with a buoy on site in season.

s1.quote: The depth of the main pool is more than 80 feet (24 m) below the surface. … constant 62 °F (17 °C) temperature

s2.publisher: City of Santa Rosa Blue Hole
s2.quote: To dive into the Blue Hole, you are required to purchase a $25 SCUBA Permit that is good for one week. … Visibility is a consistent 100 feet

access.value: SCUBA permit required ($25 per week); certification card required

summary.text: A spring-fed pool beside old Route 66 in Santa Rosa, popular for training thanks to steady cool water and long visibility. Divers buy a city permit and show a certification card; the cave passages below are gated off.

s1.publisher: California Department of Fish and Wildlife
s1.quote: diving this site is for advanced divers only due to strong currents and steep drop-offs. … a seven- to eight-hour boat ride from Ventura

s2.quote: Depths: 20 to well over 130 feet. Many sections a vertical drop to very deep water. … Visibility is generally very good, averaging 40 feet with many days of over 100.

access.value: State Marine Reserve (no-take); 7-8 hour boat ride from Ventura

summary.text: A remote pinnacle system far off San Nicolas Island, reached on long boat trips from Ventura. Sheer walls and strong current make it a dive for advanced divers, with typically very good water clarity.

s1.quote: the rocks are a common destination for local dive boats and scuba diving.
Max/Min Depths: 0' - 51' … Average Clarity: Ranges from 5' to 25'+
Cuba's wreck forms an artificial reef, and supports marine life including the California sheephead. As such, it is now a wreck diving site.

s2.quote: Today, Cuba is a popular sanctuary dive site. … The triple-expansion steam engines and boilers are still in their original upright position

highlights.text: Steam engines and boilers still upright

summary.text: A 1923 steamship wreck off San Miguel Island inside Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary. The hull is well consolidated, with engines and boilers still upright, and it now shelters local reef life.

sites.name: SS Lancing

s1.quote: Lying in about 160 feet of water, Lancing remains sitting nearly upside down on the seafloor … The hull is broken into two pieces allowing access inside the ship

penetration.value: Hull broken in two; openings allow access to the machinery space

sites.depthNote: Wreck lies in about 160 ft; pin on Wikipedia differs from NOAA position

s1.quote: Max Depth: 40-60 feet on average … Approximately 58°F year-round … often exceeding 100 feet

s2.quote: The clear, 58-degree water, illuminated from above, affords divers visibility … Diving is conducted in groups of nine, always accompanied by two guides.

access.value: Guided dives only, groups of nine with two guides

summary.text: A flooded former lead mine in Missouri, run as a guided dive resort with stadium-style lighting. Still, cool water and very long visibility let groups tour pillars, mining equipment and a flooded shaft.
